not_in_reference: Plain is not one of the 38 connectors transcribed from the reference. It was added deliberately at the user's request. Do not 'correct' the catalogue by removing it.
incomplete: The endpoint and key format are now known, so this can connect. What is still missing is READS - the thread and customer queries. A support connector that can only write is the wrong shape. See pending_operations.

shape.note: GraphQL, not REST - the first in this catalogue. There is one endpoint and one HTTP method; operations below are named mutations, and what varies is the document sent, not the path. Authorisation is per-operation permission strings rather than OAuth scopes or roles.
shape.errors: Plain returns errors INSIDE a successful response: every mutation selects an `error { message type code }` alongside its payload. A 200 with a populated error field is a failure. Code that only checks the HTTP status will read every rejection as a success - this is the single most likely way to get this connector wrong.

personal_token.label: API key
personal_token.where: Plain > Settings > Machine Users > Add Machine User, then Add API Key on that user and tick the permissions.
notes: Keys belong to a MACHINE USER, not to a person. A machine user has a Name (internal, describes the job - 'Flux') and a Public name (shown to customers if it ever interacts with them - so pick something a customer seeing it would understand).
One machine user can hold several keys, explicitly so they can be rotated without downtime. Issue a second, cut over, revoke the first.
Permissions are chosen per key at creation. Tick only thread:reply, email:create and email:read. Do NOT tick customer:impersonate - see never_expose.
Shown once. Copy it before navigating away.
When a call fails for permissions, Plain's error names the permission that was missing - so a 'you need X' error is the answer, not a puzzle.
A bare bearer key. No OAuth flow is published for this API.

Because the key is attached to a machine user, everything it does is attributable to that user rather than to a person - the same consideration as DualEntry's 'API Key' audit entries. One machine user per integration keeps the history readable.

api.schema: https://core-api.uk.plain.com/graphql/v1/schema.graphql - the full SDL, worth diffing on upgrade.
api.region_caveat: Note the `uk` in the host. Plain's published examples use the UK region, which implies other regional hosts exist and that a customer on a different region has a different URL. Confirm the right host for the account before hard-coding this one.
api.verified: search - this URL came from documentation search, not from a page supplied verbatim, unlike the auth mechanics above.
api.transport_note: ConnectorClient builds REST calls only, so no operation here is executable yet and GetStatus reports the connector as not connectable. Stated here rather than left to be inferred, so the check can tell "GraphQL, deliberately not wired" from "somebody forgot the method and path".

reply_to_thread.label: Reply to a thread
reply_to_thread.notes: Only works when the thread's `channel` is API, CHAT, EMAIL, SLACK or MS_TEAMS. Read `channel` off the thread first; otherwise the mutation fails with cannot_reply_to_thread and a message saying why.

reply_to_email.label: Reply to an email
reply_to_email.notes: Replies to one inbound email by inReplyToEmailId, rather than to the thread. Takes customerId plus both textContent and markdownContent - send both, they are the two renderings of the same message, not alternatives.

send_new_email.label: Send a new email
send_new_email.notes: Outbound, unprompted mail to a customer - Plain's own framing is proactively reaching out about issues. This is the highest-consequence operation exposed here: it starts a conversation with a real customer who did not ask for one, so it needs explicit per-send confirmation, not a standing approval.

never_expose: The `impersonation` parameter on replyToThread, and the customer:impersonate permission that enables it. It sends a message that appears to come from the customer themselves - on an EMAIL or API thread it forges their address into the From line, and in Slack and chat it wears their name and avatar. Plain built it for headless-portal products relaying a customer's own words, which is legitimate; an agent composing text and sending it as a named third party is not the same thing, and nothing in the Flux catalogue needs it. Leave customer:impersonate off the key so the capability cannot be reached even by mistake.
channelSpecificOptions.hiddenRecipients on a reply - it Bccs a third party into a customer conversation without either party seeing it.

pending_operations.note: Only the three messaging mutations whose pages were supplied are recorded. Plain's docs list considerably more, and none of it is guessed here.
wanted: Reading threads, and the queries behind them - this connector is still all writes and no reads, which is the wrong shape for a support task.
Confirmation of the regional endpoint hosts, and which one a given workspace uses.
Error handling and Error codes - the `type` and `code` vocabulary in the inline error object.
Pagination - how to page threads and customers.

also_ships.sdk: A fully typed TypeScript GraphQL SDK, plus separate webhook and UI-component SDKs.
also_ships.api_explorer: app.plain.com/developer/api-explorer - the quickest way to confirm a document and a permission set before wiring one up.
also_ships.agents: Plain documents a first-party agent story - machine users, receiving events, routing, reading threads, searching knowledge, acting on threads. Worth reading before building Flux skills against this, since it may already cover the workflow.
also_ships.security: Request signing and mTLS are both documented, which matters for the webhook direction rather than for outbound calls.

notes: The three mutations, their permission strings, the repliable channel list, the inline error shape and the impersonation behaviour are taken verbatim from Plain's own messaging pages.
The write_scope on each operation is Flux's judgement, not Plain's.
www.plain.com is not reachable from the Flux container - the egress proxy refuses the CONNECT - so the authentication and error-handling pages need supplying the same way.

The machine-user model, key rotation, per-key permissions and the plainApiKey_ prefix come from Plain's own authentication page. The endpoint URL and schema URL came from documentation search and are flagged as such on the api block - the two halves have different verification and the file says so rather than averaging them.
